title: MSF expands response to Ebola disease with new treatment centres
content:
In northeastern Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC), Médecins Sans Frontières (MSF) is expanding our response to the Ebola disease outbreak, as it spreads from the remote town of Nia Nia, in Ituri province, to Kisangani, the busy capital of neighbouring Tshopo province.
In Kisangani, MSF has been running the Ebola treatment centre (ETC) at Hôpital du Cinquantenaire, in collaboration with the Ministry of Health, since the end of June. In the first week of September, patients were transferred to a new 22-bed ETC, built and run by MSF, increasing treatment capacity in Kisangani.
In Nia Nia, MSF teams started working alongside the Ministry of Health at the ETC in the local hospital in early August. This week, MSF opened a new 50-bed ETC next to the hospital, further expanding access to Ebola care in the area.
The two locations are closely connected. Nia Nia is situated in an area with significant movement of people and goods between Ituri, Tshopo and Haut-Uele provinces. Since the first cases were reported there, people infected in or linked to Nia Nia have travelled to other areas, including Kisangani. Thirteen of the 14 positive cases recorded in Kisangani as of 1 September had an epidemiological link to Nia Nia.
Responding where the outbreak is spreading
Nia Nia has become a major focus of the outbreak in southern Ituri. The town recorded its first cases at the end of June, but the response has faced significant challenges, including limited access to healthcare, gaps in infection prevention and control, and fear and misinformation within the community.
MSF teams began working in Nia Nia in early August. As of 1 September, the Nia Nia ETC had admitted 85 people with symptoms matching Ebola. Of these, 59 were confirmed Ebola cases, including 15 patients who died. MSF opened a 50-bed ETC next to the existing facility, with 16 beds for suspected cases and 34 for confirmed cases, this week. The new centre is designed to provide safer and more effective care, with the protocols and bio-safety measures needed to treat patients with Ebola.
“In an Ebola treatment centre, what we can do is care for the individual patient, but epidemics are stopped in the community,” says Miriam Alia, MSF medical coordinator.
In an Ebola treatment centre, what we can do is care for the individual patient, but epidemics are stopped in the community.am Alia, MSF medical coordinator
When fear prevents people from seeking care
During the first weeks of the outbreak in Nia Nia, fewer patients were reaching the ETC than the number of confirmed deaths reported in the community. Many people remained at home rather than seeking care.
There are now signs of change. More people are reaching the treatment centre alive, giving them the opportunity to receive early, supportive treatment.
“Three weeks ago, we started receiving patients rather than only alerts about deaths in the community,” says Alia. “This is a major change because it means people are coming to the ETC earlier, when they develop symptoms.”
From the beginning, the response in Nia Nia has faced strong resistance, with rumours and misinformation fuelling fear. These have included claims that Ebola did not exist or that medical staff were bringing the disease into communities. Health workers were threatened, and an earlier treatment centre in the region was attacked and destroyed on 30 June.
“I didn’t believe that Ebola existed,” says Maurice, a recovered Ebola patient who was treated by MSF in Kisangani. “But when I was tested and found out that I had Ebola, that’s when I understood that it exists. But people still say that Ebola isn’t real. In my neighbourhood, in people’s homes, that’s what I used to hear.”
I didn’t believe that Ebola existed. But when I was tested and found out that I had Ebola, that’s when I understood that it exists.Maurice, a recovered Ebola patient
MSF teams are working with community leaders, health workers and other local organisations to understand concerns, address misinformation, and build acceptance of the response.
“During Ebola outbreaks, we used to talk about two epidemics: the epidemic itself, and the epidemic of fear,” says Alia. “Now we have a third one: the epidemic of misinformation.”
From Nia-Nia to Kisangani
The link between Nia Nia and Kisangani shows why containing the outbreak in hard-to-reach areas is critical.
“In the past month, two other people were infected in Kisangani after coming into contact with a body that had arrived from Nia Nia,” says Amy Low, MSF project medical adviser in Kisangani.
Also in the past week, three patients with an epidemiological link to Nia Nia died at the MSF-supported ETC in Kisangani.
MSF is expanding our capacity in both locations. But treatment centres alone cannot stop Ebola. Surveillance, testing, contact tracing, infection prevention and control, early isolation, treatment and community engagement all need to work together to reduce transmission and ensure that communities, such as Nia Nia, are not left behind.

title: Power Restoration Efforts Progress After Cuba's Electrical System Collapse
content:
On Friday, the Electric Union (UNE) shared detailed updates across provinces regarding the restoration progress following the eighth nationwide blackout of the National Electroenergetic System (SEN) in 2026, which occurred just before 2:00 PM.
The outage was caused by the sequential failure of two high-voltage lines originating from Matanzas—specifically the 220 kV Matanzas-Cienfuegos and Matanzas-Santa Clara lines—plunging the entire nation into darkness within minutes.
Efforts to restore power moved forward gradually, relying on small-scale generation systems that prioritized essential services such as hospitals, water pumping stations, and telecommunications.
Severe Power Shortages in Havana
In Havana, the situation is dire. According to the Havana Electric Company, only 11 out of 26 substations were operational at the time of the report, with just 21 out of 286 distribution circuits active.
This means a mere 63,581 customers out of 862,732 had electricity, equating to only 7.4% of the city being powered.
Of the capital's 45 hospitals, just 17 had electricity. Only one water pumping system was working out of 18 major pumping stations and supply sources.
Matanzas Utilizes Guanábana Battery for Power
The Matanzas Electric Company reported that by creating a localized grid with the Guanábana battery, they were able to supply power to two circuits: MI 1325, serving Chirimoya and the Faustino Pérez Provincial Hospital, and MI 1328, which powers the Mills, EIDE, the Fish Hatchery Station, and ECIL.
"The Provincial Load Dispatch is tirelessly working to restore electrical service in the province," the local company stated in their update.
Las Tunas Restores Power to Health Complex
In Las Tunas, the provincial electric company confirmed that by 7:17 PM, electricity had been restored to the Health Complex and part of the TK10 circuit, which supplies the Provincial Load Dispatch, via a small generation system.
Holguín Deploys Micro Grids for Essential Services
The Holguín Electric Company maintained power in critical areas using micro grids: Circuit 12, covering the Military Hospital, Pediatrics, and the Surgical Clinic; Circuit 20, which serves the Lenin Hospital, ETECSA, and the electric company itself; Alcides Pino Circuit for Communications; Circuit 18 for Guirabo Pumping; and Line 4360 for the Industrial Zone.
"Currently, we're providing electricity through micro grids to vital services," the company noted in their update.
Santa Cruz Power Plant's Unit 2 Back Online
As part of the recovery efforts, UNE confirmed that Unit 2 of the Ernesto Guevara de la Serna thermoelectric plant in Santa Cruz del Norte, Mayabeque, resumed operations, aiding the gradual restoration of the system.
This marks the eighth comprehensive failure of the SEN in 2026, with two incidents in March, three in July, two in August, and the latest on Friday.
Previous recoveries paint a bleak picture: after the fifth blackout, Havana managed only 4% service in the initial hours; after the sixth, it reached just 14% the following day. UNE has not specified a timeline for complete restoration.
Friday's collapse occurred when the system was already operating at its limits. The outage report from that day noted only 1,113 MW of available generation against a projected demand of 3,210 MW, with a maximum anticipated shortfall of 2,007 MW.
Prior to the complete blackout, Havana was experiencing 358 MW of outages across 117 circuits, while Villa Clara had 142 circuits offline and a deficit of 204 MW.
Understanding Cuba's Recurrent Blackouts
What caused the most recent collapse of the SEN in Cuba?
The most recent SEN collapse in Cuba was triggered by the successive failure of two high-voltage lines originating from Matanzas, specifically the 220 kV Matanzas-Cienfuegos and Matanzas-Santa Clara lines.
How is Cuba addressing power restoration after the blackout?
Cuba is addressing power restoration through gradual efforts utilizing small-scale generation systems. These systems prioritize essential services such as hospitals, water pumping, and telecommunications.
Why is Havana's power restoration particularly slow?
Havana's power restoration is particularly slow due to only 11 out of 26 substations being operational and just 21 out of 286 distribution circuits active. This limited capacity results in only 7.4% of the city having electricity.

title: Qatar embassy brings communities together at Ottawa fall gathering
content:
The Embassy of the State of Qatar in Ottawa welcomed members of the Qatari, Canadian and wider local communities to the Ottawa Fall Get-Together at Leamy Lake Park in Gatineau, Quebec, held as part of the 2026 Year of Culture partnership between the two countries.
Bringing together more than 100 attendees, the outdoor gathering celebrated the growing friendship between Qatar and Canada through an afternoon of sport, food and informal cultural exchange. Guests of different ages took part in basketball, volleyball and tug-of-war, creating a relaxed setting in which families and community members could meet and form new connections. Tariq Ali Faraj al-Ansari, ambassador of the State of Qatar to Canada, said: “This gathering represents an exciting manifestation of the cultural exchange between our peoples and sets an example of mutual understanding. The 2026 Year of Culture partnership goes beyond words, as we demonstrate the important nexus between culture, friendship, peace, and development.
“Our message today is that our friendship goes beyond borders, and that our cultural exchange will continue to strengthen and nurture the friendly relations between our two countries and peoples. Together, we can build peaceful and inclusive societies.”
The Qatar, Canada and Mexico 2026 Year of Culture creates opportunities for people to discover one another’s cultures and build lasting relationships. Its programme brings communities, institutions and creative practitioners together through cultural, educational, sporting and community-led activities in the partner countries.
The fall gathering’s strong turnout and warm community atmosphere demonstrated how simple shared experiences can support deeper understanding and lasting people-to-people ties between Qatar and Canada.
The Ottawa Fall Get-Together followed a wide-ranging programme of exchange between Qatar and Canada throughout 2026. In Canada, the Year of Culture was launched with a dedicated media day at the Embassy of Qatar in Ottawa; M7 introduced emerging designers from Qatar to Canadian audiences at Fashion Art Toronto; Qatari artist Ghada al-Suwaidi created a special helmet worn by Pierre Gasly at the Formula 1 Canadian Grand Prix in Montreal; and calligraffiti artist Fatima al-Sharshani produced a public artwork for Montreal’s MURAL Festival. In Toronto, Doha Debates brought together students and voices from sport and media for a Town Hall exploring football fandom, community and commercialisation.
In Qatar, Canadian chefs Christian Gosselin, Eric Chong and Andy Hay shared the country’s diverse culinary traditions at the Qatar International Food Festival, while Canadian artists participated in the inaugural Art Basel Qatar.
Canada’s sporting culture was also celebrated through street curling on National Sport Day and a wider winter sports programme featuring ice hockey, curling and skating, alongside Canadian community participation and cultural activities.
Together, these exchanges have connected artists, designers, chefs, young people, athletes and families, creating new opportunities for Qataris and Canadians to experience one another’s cultures and build lasting relationships.

title: Iran mobilisation drive extends to children under 15
content:
Four years have passed since Zhina Mahsa Amini, a 22-year-old woman who had travelled to Tehran to visit family, died after being detained by the morality police.
She could never have imagined how her name would appear on walls, streets and university campuses, or on the lips of millions of Iranians, or how three simple words, “Woman, Life, Freedom,” would become one of the most enduring slogans in Iran’s modern history.
The story of 2022 is not only the story of a slogan. It is the story of the price thousands paid to break through the wall of fear.
Zhina’s death on September 16, 2022, sparked protests across Iran. Human rights organizations documented live ammunition and pellet fire, mass arrests, torture, sexual violence and the killing of protesters. HRANA later recorded protests in all 31 provinces, 160 cities and 143 universities, and reported at least 530 people killed, including 68 children and teenagers.
Nika Shakarami and Sarina Esmailzadeh were both sixteen. Kian Pirfalak was nine, remembered for “In the name of the God of the rainbow” and the small boat he built with his own hands. Khodanour Lojei, a 27-year-old Baluch man, lives on in videos of him dancing, alongside the haunting image of him with his hands tied to a pole and water placed before him while in detention.
Their stories were different, but each became part of the collective memory of Woman, Life, Freedom.
Then came the gallows. Mohammad Mehdi Karami, a 22-year-old karate champion, was executed after being sentenced in connection with the fortieth-day commemoration for Hadis Najafi. Seyed Mohammad Hosseini, who worked at a poultry farm and taught martial arts to disadvantaged children for free, was executed the same day; human rights reports say his confessions were obtained under torture. Majidreza Rahnavard, executed only 23 days after his arrest, asked before his death that people not cry at his grave but celebrate and play happy music.
These names are reminders that behind every statistic was a family.
The repression did not end with the street protests. Students, schoolchildren, journalists, artists, athletes and activists were arrested. Families sometimes went weeks or months without news. Some detainees appeared in televised “confessions” that human rights organizations said were tainted by torture. Families seeking the truth about those killed also faced pressure. Others eventually left Iran after imprisonment, threats and persecution, carrying the cost of the uprising into exile, lost careers, interrupted education and separation from family.
And yet one of the movement’s deepest legacies is visible in an ordinary scene: a woman walking down an Iranian street without compulsory hijab.
The state responded with fines, vehicle seizures, arrests, flogging, business closures, cameras and surveillance. But women’s defiance continued. Four years after Zhina’s death, a woman without compulsory hijab is no longer the exceptional image it was in September 2022; it has become part of Iran’s social reality.
That is also where the connection to Dey 1404 (December 2025 and January 2026) becomes important.
The new protests began amid the collapse of the currency, inflation and protests by Tehran bazaar merchants, but quickly moved beyond economic demands. According to HRANA data cited in a UK government report, by January 27 at least 656 gatherings had been recorded in 201 cities across all 31 provinces, compared with 160 cities during the 1401 protests.
There are no reliable data to compare total participation, but the later uprising was documented across more cities and had a far higher reported toll. By March 2026, HRANA had recorded information on more than 7,000 people killed and more than 53,000 arrested in connection with the Dey and Bahman protests, far above the Iranian government’s figures.
HRANA described the confirmed cases as the minimum it could verify, with thousands more still awaiting review. Internet shutdowns, pressure on families and the lack of independent access inside Iran made the full scale harder to establish.
But the difference was not only scale. The society that entered January 2026 was not the same society that had existed before September 2022.
Iranians had lived through a national experience of disobedience, broken taboos, solidarity, bullets, prison, executions, migration and grief.
Abolfazl Hajizadegan’s research on “The Lives of Dey,” based on the social-media traces of 957 of those killed, found people from widely different professions and backgrounds, from baristas, repair workers and sports coaches to lawyers, professors, filmmakers and musicians.
The uprising also entered families in ways that made the breadth of the upheaval painfully visible.
Mehdi Shafiei, 44, and his 18-year-old son Mani were killed in Eslamshahr less than two hours apart. In Bushehr, 37-year-old nurse Mansoureh Heydari and her husband, Behrouz Mansouri, were both killed, leaving behind two children. Elsewhere, fathers and daughters were arrested together.
This does not mean that the 1401 and 1404 uprisings were identical, or that all protesters shared one ideology, leader or vision of Iran’s future. Their immediate triggers were different. But something had changed in society’s relationship with fear.
Repression continued, but the memory of disobedience could not simply be erased. Hajizadegan’s research suggests that those who came into the streets in 1404 did not acquire their anger overnight. Their earlier posts showed dissatisfaction and protest stretching back through previous protest waves, including the November 2019 protests and the 2022 uprising.
Dey 1404 was therefore not simply the explosion of an economic crisis. It was part of a longer accumulation of experience. Perhaps this is one of the most important legacies Woman, Life, Freedom left behind: not a single organization or leadership, but a social experience of the possibility of saying “no.”
The government’s response in Dey 1404 was severe. From January 8, the internet was almost completely shut down. Amnesty International reported widespread killings, mass arrests, enforced disappearances, torture and systematic pressure on victims’ families.
Yet behind every new number was another life: Hamid Mahdavi, Mohammad Jabbari, Mehdi and Mani, Mansoureh and Behrouz, just as Nika, Sarina, Kian and Khodanour had been lives, not statistics, four years earlier.
From September 2022 to January 2026, the names and faces changed and the sparks were different, but each chapter left something for the next: memory, wounds, language, courage and sometimes hope.
Zhina is not only the name of a young woman, and Woman, Life, Freedom is not merely the name of a few months of protest. It became part of the social and political language of a generation that paid an extraordinarily heavy price and emerged with a different understanding of choice, dignity and the possibility of standing firm.
Zhina and thousands of others killed in Iran’s protest movements are no longer with us. But something of them remains: in the hair of a woman who chooses not to cover it; in a mother who refuses to let her child’s name be erased; in a father who rejects the official account of his son’s death; in a family that dances at a loved one’s grave despite threats; and in a generation that has not abandoned its questions about freedom, dignity and the future.
Repression can empty the streets for a time, but it cannot erase what a generation has lived through.

title: There’s no ‘best’ diet for healthy aging, study suggests
content:
Several healthy dietary patterns have been tied to living longer in good health.
The Mediterranean, DASH, MIND and plant-based diets, for example, have all been associated with a lower risk of chronic disease and premature death.
With so many recommended healthy eating plans, each differing somewhat in the foods they highlight, you might wonder if one is a better choice for healthy aging than the others.
According to a large new study, when it comes to “biological aging,” no single healthy dietary pattern appears to have a clear advantage.
Here’s a breakdown of the research, and why you needn’t worry about choosing the “best” healthy diet.
What is biological aging?
Biological age is an estimate of how fast or slow your cells, tissues and organ systems are aging, rather than simply how many years you have lived.
Eat these foods to promote heart health
It’s influenced by genetics, health status, diet, physical activity, sleep habits, smoking and alcohol use and stress.
One method used to estimate biological age involves using epigenetic clocks, tools that analyze small chemical tags on DNA called methylation markers. These markers change in predictable ways with age and may influence how cells function, repair themselves and respond to stress.
About the new research
The study, published Aug. 29, in the journal Nature Communications, investigated whether adhering to 10 dietary patterns was associated with slower biological aging, and whether these diets influence similar or different biological pathways in the body.
To do so, the researchers analyzed data from the ongoing Rhineland Study involving 6,470 adults, with an average age of 56, who were living in Bonn, Germany.
Participants of that study completed a detailed questionnaire about their usual diets over the previous year. This information was then used to calculate 10 separate diet quality scores.
Specifically, the researchers assessed how closely each person’s usual diet matched 10 dietary patterns: Mediterranean diet, DASH diet, MIND diet, Alternative Healthy Eating Index (AHEI), Nordic diet, EAT-Lancet diet, Plant-based Diet Index, Healthy Plant-based Diet Index, Unhealthy Plant-based Diet Index and the Dietary Inflammatory Index.
The healthy diet patterns evaluated share many features, but they can also differ in the type of fat emphasized, dairy product intake, fish consumption, red meat restrictions and alcohol recommendations.
Participants’ biological age was measured using three different epigenic clocks.
Healthy diets tied to slower biological aging
Higher adherence to the Mediterranean, DASH, MIND, AHEI, Nordic and healthy plant-based diets were all associated with slower biological aging.
Higher adherence to unhealthy inflammatory dietary patterns, on the other hand, were linked to faster biological aging.
An anti-inflammatory diet may prevent dementia, even in people at higher risk, new study suggests
Among all dietary patterns examined, the DASH and Nordic diets were consistently associated with slower biological aging across all three measures.
To see if the findings held up, the researchers repeated the analysis for 1,034 adults participating in a separate German study called EPIC-Potsdam, and found similar results.
The study was observational and found associations; it didn’t prove that healthier diets slowed aging.
Still, the study’s large sample size, assessment of 10 dietary patterns rather than only one, use of multiple biological aging measures, and similar results found in a second study add weight to the conclusions.
The findings are intriguing, but they’re not totally unexpected. Plenty of evidence has linked healthier dietary patterns to a lower risk of chronic disease and healthier aging.
The current study adds to that knowledge by showing healthy diets are also associated with markers of slower biological aging.
Key takeaway
There was one surprising, and perhaps reassuring, finding.
The researchers found that different dietary patterns were each associated with distinct patterns of DNA methylation markers.
Despite these differences, many of the healthy dietary patterns appeared to influence the same biological pathways linked to how cells communicate, grow, function and maintain themselves.
In other words, while the healthy diets may not work in exactly the same way, they seem to influence the same underlying processes associated with healthy aging.
The takeaway is that there isn’t only one optimal way to eat well.
Instead, it appears that several healthy eating patterns that emphasize different combinations of foods support healthy aging.
To me, that’s the important message to take from this study.
Instead of worrying about following the “best” dietary pattern or following it perfectly, perhaps it’s more important to focus on what these diets have in common.
That means consistently eating a diet plentiful in vegetables, fruit, whole grains, pulses, nuts and minimally processed foods.
Leslie Beck, a Toronto-based private practice dietitian, is director of food and nutrition at Medcan.

title: BE "evolui posição" e abstém-se em voto de pesar por Sadokha
content:
Depois de ter acompanhado o voto de pesar pela morte de Pavlo Sadokha na Assembleia Municipal de Lisboa, o Bloco de Esquerda absteve-se em iniciativas com o mesmo objeto na Assembleia da República e na Câmara de Lisboa. Já o PCP manteve o seu voto contra o pesar pela morte do presidente de longa data da Associação dos Ucranianos em Portugal no dia 13 de setembro.
O vereador Ricardo Moreira explica ao Observador que o BE “evoluiu de posição” após contactos com “democratas ucranianos” e que a abstenção esta quarta-feira na CML está alinhada com o voto da deputada Andreia Galvão no Parlamento na sexta-feira. Ao contrário do PCP, o BE tem maioritariamente votado ao lado dos restantes partidos em iniciativas políticas a favor da Ucrânia e de condenação da Rússia desde a invasão em 2022. Os bloquistas reafirmam a “inequívoca condenação da invasão russa da Ucrânia”, mas justificam a abstenção neste caso com o “percurso público” do antigo líder da Associação dos Ucranianos em Portugal.
“O percurso público de Pavlo Sadokha ficou também marcado por posições e referências políticas com as quais o Bloco de Esquerda mantém profundas divergências, que não podem ser ignoradas ou apagadas”, lê-se na declaração de voto escrita entregue por Ricardo Moreira. “A nossa abstenção exprime simultaneamente o respeito pela dor da sua família, dos seus amigos e da comunidade ucraniana em Portugal, bem como a convicção de que a solidariedade que devemos ao povo da Ucrânia inclui todos os democratas e antifascistas que resistem à agressão russa”, conclui.
O percurso político de Pavlo Sadokha, cuja morte aos 56 anos está a ser investigada pelo Ministério Público, também foi o principal motivo evocado pelos comunistas para justificarem o voto contra. Segundo o site AbrilAbril, plataforma da responsabilidade do PCP, Sadokha foi assessor do deputado Yuriy Syrotiuk, membro do partido de extrema-direita Svoboda, inspirado na controversa figura de Stepan Bandera. O ex-líder da Associação dos Ucranianos em Portugal, que também tinha ligações a movimentos como os Azov ou Setor Direito, rejeita ligações ao nazismo.
O voto de pesar apresentado esta quarta-feira pela coligação liderada por Carlos Moedas destaca que Pavlo Sadokha residia há mais de duas décadas em Portugal. “Destacou-se pela ação cívica e humanitária a que se dedicava intensivamente. Teve um papel preponderante na preservação da identidade cultural da sua comunidade, no apoio aos imigrantes e na promoção do diálogo intercultural e de solidariedade no concelho de Lisboa.” Sadokha, militante do PSD, foi também candidato à Assembleia Municipal de Lisboa e à assembleia de freguesia de São Domingos de Benfica nas eleições autárquicas de 2025.
Morreu Pavlo Sadokha, presidente da Associação dos Ucranianos em Portugal

title: South Korea’s new agrivoltaics law sets 30-year permit ceiling
content:
South Korea’s new agrivoltaics law sets 30-year permit ceiling
South Korea’s Ministry of Agriculture, Food and Rural Affairs (MAFRA) said this week that the country has issued a new agrivoltaics law, set to take effect Dec. 17, following the bill’s passage through the National Assembly in May.
The law creates the country’s first dedicated legal framework for combining solar generation with continued agricultural production. MAFRA is responsible for implementing the act.
The enacted statute sets a maximum project period of up to 30 years, which is an increase from the 23-year framework reported when the bill passed the National Assembly.
The precise duration granted to any individual project will be determined by local authorities under a future presidential decree, according to ministry statements. The 30-year ceiling replaces South Korea’s previous eight-year temporary land-use permit regime, which researchers had identified as a barrier to project financing.
The law restricts eligibility to operate an agrivoltaic project to three categories. The first is local farmers who have continuously resided in the relevant area and can demonstrate at least three years of agricultural management. The second is resident-participation cooperatives formed by at least 10 local residents. The third is qualifying agricultural corporations operating within designated renewable energy zones.
The law does not necessarily bar all forms of external capital or financing arrangements – it specifically restricts who may hold the licensed project-operator status. Eligible farmland is limited to land outside Agricultural Promotion Zones, or land within those zones that has been separately designated a Renewable Energy Zone, a designation established under South Korea’s framework on the restructuring of rural spaces.
The nonprofit group Solutions for Our Climate said in May that Agricultural Promotion Zones cover approximately 47% of South Korea’s total farmland, a figure drawn from external land-use data rather than the statute itself. The enacted law does not restate or revise that estimate; it only sets the legal pathway by which land in such zones could become eligible.
The law requires project operators to continue agricultural production every year under an approved farming plan, and imposes maintenance and record-keeping obligations on the underlying solar equipment. But the legislation leaves the technical details to a presidential decree that hasn’t been issued yet – things like exact limits on shading, how tall structures can be, spacing between supports.
What the law itself says now appears to be narrower in scope. Ultimately, local authorities have to check that a project’s structure does not block farm machinery or cut off too much sunlight.
Policy and industry materials have floated a shading limit near 30%, minimum structure heights around 2.5 meters and support spacing near 4 meters as likely benchmarks, though none of these figures are confirmed requirements of the enacted law.
South Korea now joins a small group of countries with dedicated agrivoltaics legislation. France’s 2023 APER law set a national legal definition for agrivoltaics, including a requirement that yields on covered land stay at roughly 90% of a reference plot, but questions remain in France over how agrivoltaic project revenues are shared with local communities.
Italy’s framework also requires sites to maintain at least 80% of standard agricultural output, but its thresholds differ from South Korea’s. Japan, meanwhile, has run a national agrivoltaics guidance framework since 2021, but its rules stop short of a dedicated statute.
The new South Korean law arrives as the country moves to expand financial support for dual-use solar. MAFRA has proposed nearly doubling government funding for factory rooftop solar and agrivoltaics to KRW 1.8 trillion ($1.3 billion) in a newly issued 2027 budget, and the country’s largest single-site solar project under development, the Haenam solar complex, includes 10 MW earmarked as agricultural PV capacity.

title: 'I thought it would make the team special' - a papal blessing with a difference
content:
'I thought it would make the team special' - a papal blessing with a difference
- Published
Wearing a special jersey on the day of the big game, sitting in the exact same seat match after match, or maybe donning some lucky underpants.
These are just some of the rituals sports fans believe can help their team win.
But 10-year-old Eoghan decided it was time to step up his fan game.
For him, the best chance to ensure success would be to wear his Tyrone GAA colours while meeting Pope Leo XIV.
"I was wearing the jersey because I thought it would make Tyrone special."
Eoghan, along with his older sister Áine and mum Edel Quinn, met the Pope in August after a friend arranged tickets to one of his weekly public audiences.
Áine says they did not realise how close they were going to be to the pontiff until they arrived at St Peter's Basilica in Vatican City.
"They led us up to the very front, we were gobsmacked."
The Castlederg family were even more surprised when they found out they would have a chance to chat with Pope Leo.
Eoghan says he shook his hand first, then Áine's and then their mum's.
"He was looking at the jersey wondering where it was from."
Áine says the Pope then acknowledged how far they had travelled.
Eoghan thinks the Pope may have recognised the jersey, as this was not the first time he came into contact with one.
In November 2025, Aidan Gallagher tossed a Tyrone jersey with 'Leo 14' written on the back of it to the pontiff outside the Vatican.
And the Tyrone connection did not stop once the meeting was over.
After receiving a blessing from the Pope and rosary beads from one of the guards, Áine says they were escorted down an aisle where hundreds of people were watching them from behind barricades.
From out of nowhere, someone in the crowd shouted "up Tyrone!".
"I could not believe it walking down seeing all those different faces and then someone says up Tyrone."
Besides the excitement of meeting the Pope, it was also an emotional day for the siblings, as Edel has Multiple Sclerosis
"Our faith is important to us, we always went to mass every Saturday or Sunday and my mum has MS, so the trip was very special for her," says Áine.
The family still cannot not believe it really happened.
Eoghan says his friends have all been asking him: "How do you shake hands with the Pope?"
While Áine says people have grabbing the hand the pontiff shook: "Being just two ordinary people from Castlederg, sitting inches from the Pope and meeting him, it was surreal."

title: New York beachgoers, lifeguards rush to save raccoon clinging above the waves
content:
An early morning beach walk in Glen Cove became a rescue effort after people spotted a raccoon clinging above the bay, shivering as waves broke below.
Residents and lifeguards at the beach chose to act, using whatever was available to help the animal back onto safe ground, according to Patch.
Here's what to know
After the raccoon was discovered at Morgan Memorial Park Beach in Glen Cove, Liz Glaviano contacted a wildlife rescue group and tried to steer it toward shore.
Mark Glaviano went to get lifeguards and summon additional help.
The animal was stuck above the water with little space to get out on its own.
Teenage lifeguards Dylan Jenkins and Taylor, along with beach worker José Benitez, joined the effort.
Using a board, Benitez helped direct the raccoon, while 19-year-old Jenkins held an umbrella underneath in case it slipped.
More background
Eventually, the raccoon latched onto the board and reached safety.
Liz Glaviano said the sight was difficult to watch.
"It just broke my heart," she said, per Patch. "I couldn't leave that little guy. He was in distress and shaking. If he lost his grip, he would have been in the waves. He just needed us to help."
How the raccoon ended up trapped is still not known.
Roni Jenkins, Dylan Jenkins' mother, described the animal as a young raccoon in distress, Patch reported.
"The poor little thing was shaking and clearly exhausted and scared," she said.
What's being done?
Those involved alerted lifeguards, contacted a wildlife rescue organization, and relied on basic equipment to help the raccoon without cornering it.
"Thankfully, everyone pitched in, and we saved him," Liz Glaviano told Patch.
Where can I learn more?
The Glen Cove rescue is one example of how fast a tense moment with wildlife can unfold on the water. Here are a few other stories involving encounters with raccoons and coastal animals, including situations where people made a stressful scene even worse.
• At one home, 100 raccoons crowded a yard after years of being fed there.
• On a California trail, hikers startled a coyote near the beach and panicked.
• At a crowded beach, tourists scattered after a sea lion charged them at close range.
• Off California, a surfer faced a vicious sea lion attack in open water.
• Locals watched a pelican coated in oil struggle along a polluted shore.

title: ABUMET Opens New Digital Learning Opportunities For Kano Pupils With Modern ICT Centre
content:
Latest Headlines
ABUMET Opens New Digital Learning Opportunities For Kano Pupils With Modern ICT Centre
Bennett Oghifo
In a major investment in education and community development, Nigeria’s leading glass and aluminium solutions company, ABUMET, has donated a fully equipped digital learning centre to Race Course Model Primary School, Kano, giving hundreds of pupils access to modern technology and practical computer education for the first time.
The initiative is part of ABUMET’s commitment to improving educational outcomes and helping young Nigerians acquire the digital skills needed to succeed in an increasingly technology-driven world.
To bring the project to life, the company provided the school with 24 desktop computers, solar-powered electricity infrastructure, and new classroom furniture for both pupils and teachers. The intervention is already creating a more conducive learning environment and introducing learners to hands-on computer education in ways that were previously difficult to achieve.
For many of the pupils, the facility represents a first meaningful encounter with digital technology, opening new possibilities for learning, creativity and future career development.
Speaking during the Corporate Social Responsibility (CSR) visit to the school, ABUMET General Manager, Diemo Schillack, said the project was inspired by the company’s desire to help bridge the digital divide and ensure that children are not left behind in the modern knowledge economy.
According to him, exposure to technology at an early age can significantly influence a child’s educational journey, build confidence and create opportunities that extend far beyond the classroom. We believe every child deserves access to quality learning tools and the opportunity to develop skills that will prepare them for the future,” Schillack said, adding, technology is now part of everyday life, and introducing these young learners to digital tools early gives them a stronger foundation for their education and future careers.
The ABUMET General Manager expressed appreciation for the warm welcome received from the pupils and staff, describing their enthusiasm and excitement as inspiring. He also reaffirmed the company’s commitment to supporting education and community development, saying that ABUMET plans to return within a year to assess the pupils’ progress and the impact of the learning centre.
The Head Teacher of Race Course Model Primary School, Salisu Alhassan, thanked ABUMET on behalf of the school’s management, teachers, pupils, parents and community stakeholders, describing the intervention as a transformative addition to the school’s educational resources.
“On behalf of all stakeholders, we sincerely appreciate ABUMET for this remarkable contribution to our school,” Alhassan said. “The computers, solar power facilities and learning furniture will greatly improve teaching and learning, particularly in the area of digital literacy, he said.
Alhassan explained that the school’s digital learning programme has been carefully structured to ensure that pupils gain practical experience with the computers despite the school’s large enrolment.
“We organise the pupils into smaller groups so that everyone has the opportunity to participate and learn, adding, this initiative goes beyond simply teaching children how to use computers. We want them to understand how technology can support learning, problem-solving and everyday life.
According to the head teacher, pupils are already learning to use applications such as Microsoft Office while developing practical skills in writing, calculations, record-keeping and information management. He added that computer education becomes more advanced from Primary Four to Primary Six, allowing pupils to progressively build their digital competence before moving to secondary school.
Established in 1996, Race Course Model Primary School currently serves about 600 pupils across 14 classrooms, offering education from Early Childhood Care and Education (ECC) through Primary.

title: Candidatos não podem ser presos a partir deste sábado (19); legislação prevê exceção para flagrante
content:
A partir deste sábado (19), candidatas e candidatos registrados para disputar as Eleições 2026 não podem ser presos ou detidos em todo o país. A medida, estabelecida pelo artigo 236 do Código Eleitoral, passa a vigorar 15 dias antes do primeiro turno da votação, marcado para 4 de outubro, e se estende até 6 de outubro, 48 horas após o encerramento do pleito.
A regra visa garantir o livre exercício da campanha eleitoral e evitar que prisões com motivações políticas interfiram na igualdade do processo democrático.
A legislação estabelece que a imunidade temporária não é absoluta, mantendo a permissão para prisões em caso de flagrante delito. Segundo o Código de Processo Penal, a exceção se aplica a indivíduos pegos cometendo a infração, recém-saídos da prática do crime, perseguidos em situação que indique autoria ou localizados com instrumentos relacionados ao delito.
Prisões decorrentes de crimes eleitorais praticados durante a campanha ou no dia da votação, como compra de votos e boca de urna, também permanecem autorizadas sob a condição de flagrante.
A restrição de prisão abrange ainda mesárias, mesários e fiscais de partidos políticos durante o exercício de suas funções. No entanto, a norma não interrompe o andamento de investigações, processos judiciais em curso ou julgamentos contra os postulantes, restringindo apenas a execução de prisões durante o período.
Caso ocorra a detenção de algum candidato em situação de flagrante, o detido deve ser conduzido imediatamente à presença de um juiz.
Para as disputas que chegarem ao segundo turno, agendado para 25 de outubro, a proteção voltará a valer em 10 de outubro para os candidatos que continuarem no pleito, seguindo até 27 de outubro.
Já para os eleitores, a restrição de prisão começa a valer mais tarde, a partir de 29 de setembro, cinco dias antes da votação, estendendo-se também até 48 horas após o encerramento do primeiro turno.

title: JOJ-2026 : Dakar fait sa toilette avant l’arrivée des délégations
content:
JOJ-2026 : Dakar fait sa toilette avant l’arrivée des délégations
À quelques semaines des JOJ Dakar-2026, la capitale accélère sa préparation. Ce dimanche 20 septembre, la plage de la Cour de cassation a accueilli une grande opération de nettoyage réunissant la Ville de Dakar, le COJOJ, l’Union européenne et plusieurs communes. Au-delà du coup de propre, l’ambition est de préparer un cadre accueillant pour les délégations et de faire de cette mobilisation un héritage des Jeux.
Les JOJ approchent et la préparation ne se joue pas uniquement sur les sites de compétition. Le cadre de vie aussi entre dans la course. Ce dimanche, élus, agents municipaux, jeunes, partenaires et populations se sont mobilisés pour nettoyer la plage de la Cour de cassation dans le cadre du "World Clean Up Day".
À l’approche de ce rendez-vous international, chaque détail compte. Et la propreté des espaces publics en fait partie. Pour Khadija Sarr, responsable des opérations urbaines au COJOJ, il faut désormais « préparer la ville, nettoyer la ville, aménager la ville, embellir la ville pour les accueillir ». Et la mobilisation dépasse largement cette plage.
Selon elle, une dizaine des 19 communes ont répondu à l’appel en menant, elles aussi, des actions de nettoiement. Un mouvement collectif qui veut donner le ton avant l’arrivée des délégations.
Un coup de propre, mais surtout un héritage
L’objectif affiché n’est toutefois pas de faire disparaître les déchets le temps d’une journée. Les organisateurs veulent installer une dynamique appelée à se poursuivre après les Jeux. « On souhaite que ce sera en continu jusqu’à la fin des Jeux et rester aussi en héritage », explique Khadija Sarr.
Une ambition partagée par l’Union européenne. Présent lors de l’opération, son chargé d’affaires au Sénégal, Thomas Eguebarth, a insisté sur la responsabilité collective dans la protection de l’environnement.
Le partenariat ne s’arrête d’ailleurs pas à cette journée. Il s’inscrit dans une coopération plus large autour de l’environnement et du développement urbain, notamment avec les actions engagées pour la dépollution de la baie de Hann et le développement de transports publics durables.
Pour Dieynaba Ba Dème, maire de Fann-Point E-Amitié et représentante du maire de Dakar, la propreté ne peut cependant pas reposer uniquement sur les opérations de terrain. « Une opération de nettoyage aussi importante soit-elle ne peut suffire à elle seule », rappelle-t-elle, plaidant pour plus de sensibilisation et de responsabilité citoyenne.
À l’heure où les premiers visiteurs commencent déjà à arriver, le compte à rebours est lancé. Nettoyer, embellir, sensibiliser : la capitale veut offrir le meilleur visage possible pour les JOJ. Mais le véritable succès de cette mobilisation se mesurera surtout après les Jeux, lorsque les projecteurs se seront éteints.

title: Incendio de gran magnitud se registró en edificio de la avenida principal de El Cementerio
content:
En horas de la tarde de este domingo un voraz incendio se desató en un edificio ubicado en la avenida principal de la parroquia El Cementerio, en Caracas, generando conmoción entre los vecinos del sector y movilizando de inmediato a los cuerpos de emergencia.
El Cuerpo de Bomberos de Caracas confirmó a través de sus redes sociales que la estructura afectada es el llamado "Edificio Mostaza", situado en las cercanías del Mercado La Hormiga, y destacó la rapidez con la que sus unidades acudieron al lugar.
"Ante la voracidad del fuego, que afecta el segundo y tercer nivel de esta edificación utilizada como depósito, las valientes comisiones priorizaron de inmediato la preservación de la vida, logrando el desalojo preventivo y exitoso de aproximadamente 30 personas de las residencias adyacentes, demostrando un nivel de pericia, valentía y protección ciudadana absoluto", se detalló.
"La inmediata movilización de nuestras unidades de supresión y equipos especializados demuestra el nivel de alerta permanente y la capacidad de respuesta de nuestra institución para actuar en zonas de alta densidad comercial y salvaguardar la vida de la ciudadanía", destacaron a través de su cuenta en la red social Instagram.
La institución explicó, además, cómo se desarrolló el trabajo de los efectivos sobre el terreno para contener el fuego y evitar que se extienda a otras edificaciones cercanas.
Al respecto, aclaró que para extinguir las llamas se siguieron los "estrictos protocolos de seguridad. Es por ello, que señalaron que los efectivos "se mantienen en el sitio realizando intensas maniobras de confinamiento y extinción para cortar el avance del fuego y evitar su propagación hacia las estructuras vecinas".
Sobre el estado actual de la emergencia y el compromiso de continuar hasta lograr el control total del incendio, el Cuerpo de Bomberos de Caracas fue enfático en su mensaje.
Afirmaron que los bomberos "se mantienen en primera línea de combate y no descansarán hasta mitigar por completo las llamas y declarar la zona en total seguridad para la comunidad".
Las imágenes que circulan en redes sociales muestran una densa nube de humo negro y la intensidad de las llamas saliendo de la edificación, una situación que ha captado la atención de residentes y transeúntes de la zona.
Hasta el momento se desconocen las causas que originaron el siniestro, y las autoridades no han reportado víctimas fatales ni heridos como consecuencia del incendio.

title: How modern tech aids Philippines disaster preparedness
content:
How modern tech aids Philippines disaster preparedness
MANILA, Philippines — Modern technology is increasingly aiding disaster preparedness in the Philippines, with the Department of Science and Technology (DOST) advancing artificial intelligence (AI) and other technologies to help save lives even before disasters strike.
AI is powering the government’s central monitoring platform, the Handa Integrated Platform for Preparedness and Response, which was launched in March to provide information on disaster preparedness across different hazards.
“It’s like the ChatGPT of disaster preparedness,” Philippine Institute of Volcanology and Seismology (PHIVOLCS) director Teresito Bacolcol said at the Cagayan Valley Regional Science, Technology and Innovation Week press conference.
“You can type in what the different active faults are in Region 2 or any part of the country, and it will provide you with answers,” he added.
Bacolcol said the Handa platform has “simplified the assessment of hazards.”
The public can access the platform at handa.georisk.gov.ph.
Anyone can submit an incident report, which will be verified by the Office of Civil Defense and local government units with accounts provided by PHIVOLCS.
AI is also being used to improve weather forecasting by the Philippine Atmospheric, Geophysical and Astronomical Services Administration.
“PAGASA’s data are so big, so we need to use AI to improve forecasts; our target is five days to 14 days,” DOST Secretary Renato Solidum Jr. said. “The computing time to process the data would be every three hours. We are experimenting with the use of AI to shorten it to 15 minutes so that the forecasts are more up-to-date.”
PAGASA recently released its National Hydro-Met Observing Network, or PANaHON app, which provides near-real-time information from weather stations across the country.
DOST has also turned over a unit of the Mobile Command and Control Vehicle (MoCCoV) to the Tuguegarao local government.
The MoCCoV is a mobile command center that can be set up in remote areas in just 20 minutes.
It has three air-conditioned rooms that can serve as a command room, conference room, rescue or medical triage room, kitchen or independent bathroom.
It is also equipped with solar panels and a backup generator that can run for up to 32 hours.
In a speech to policymakers and disaster responders, Solidum said DOST is committed to investing in scientific research, hazard monitoring, early warning systems, geospatial technologies, impact-based forecasting and AI to allow the public to act with greater knowledge and lead time.
“But our responsibility at the DOST goes beyond producing information,” Solidum said. “Science must enter the decisions that shape people’s lives … Science and the information it provides must guide policies and influence investment.”
“The public expects information to move and decisions to be made. They expect resources to reach the people who need them. And they expect us to be ready before the emergency begins; that’s why convergence should produce a connected and operationally ready disaster risk reduction and management system,” he added.

title: Top court allows bail for specialised medical care
content: The Supreme Court has held that an undertrial prisoner suffering from an ailment requiring specialised treatment and medical supervision unavailable in jail may be granted post-arrest bail on medical grounds, particularly where continued detention could pose a serious risk to his health or life. A three-member bench headed by Justice Shahid Waheed passed the ruling while allowing two petitions filed by Zeeshan Majeed Bhatti seeking bail on medical grounds, granting him post-arrest bail in both cases. In its detailed judgment, the court observed that medical reports submitted by the Medical Officer of Central Jail, Rawalpindi, showed that the accused was suffering from serious ailments and was not receiving the specialised treatment required at the jail hospital. The accused was suffering from hypertension, diabetes and cardiac problems, besides complaints of chest pain. Cardiologists had recommended specialised medical examination and treatment, the judgment noted. The apex court observed that the ailments suffered by the accused required specialised treatment and continuous medical supervision, which could not be adequately provided by the jail authorities. It held that continued detention without the required specialised treatment could adversely affect the accused's health and could also pose a danger to his life. Referring to its earlier judgments concerning bail on medical grounds, the court held that post-arrest bail could be granted.

title: Fazer memória das lutas e educar para os direitos humanos é o caminho para a transformação
content:
Por Priscila Costa Porcidônio e Maria Marques
Falar de direitos humanos é resgatar a própria história das lutas da humanidade. Eles não caíram do céu, nem surgiram prontos em gabinetes. Pelo contrário, foram sendo forjados passo a passo, no calor das resistências contra a violência, a desigualdade extrema, a exploração e a negação da liberdade.
Durante séculos, populações inteiras foram marginalizadas e privadas de dignidade por conta de sua origem, cor da pele, gênero, religião ou classe social. Foi preciso que o mundo testemunhasse atrocidades indescritíveis, cujos ápices se deram nos conflitos do século XX, para que a comunidade internacional firmasse, por meio da Declaração Universal dos Direitos Humanos (1948), um pacto civilizatório inegociável: todas as pessoas nascem livres e iguais em dignidade e direitos.
No entanto, sabemos que a proclamação de uma lei não garante, por si só, a sua efetivação na vida real.
No Brasil, essa história de lutas ganha contornos ainda mais dramáticos. Carregamos as feridas abertas de mais de três séculos de escravização — que estruturam nossas desigualdades socioeconômicas até os dias de hoje — e as marcas da censura e da retirada de direitos deixadas pela ditadura militar. A Constituição de 1988 representou um respiro democrático e um marco na garantia dos direitos sociais, mas a realidade cotidiana insiste em nos mostrar que a luta não terminou.
Hoje, vivenciamos o recrudescimento da violência, do racismo, da intolerância religiosa, das desigualdades e do machismo. Povos indígenas, a população negra, migrantes, pessoas LGBTQIAPN+, pessoas com deficiência e outros grupos historicamente marginalizados continuam sendo alvos de negação de direitos.
Somado a isso, a disseminação de discursos de ódio e “fake news” nas redes sociais ameaça diretamente o tecido democrático, dificultando o diálogo e a construção da verdade.
Como enfrentar, então, essa realidade tão complexa?
A resposta passa, obrigatoriamente, pela Educação em Direitos Humanos (EDH). Uma educação verdadeiramente comprometida com esse tema não se limita a transmitir conteúdos; ela é uma ferramenta de intervenção social. Ensina a problematizar as injustiças, a resolver conflitos de forma não violenta e a valorizar ativamente a diversidade.
Aprender e respirar os Direitos Humanos nos espaços educativos não é apenas acumular leituras, mas passar por uma desconstrução profunda de como enxergamos a sala de aula e a sociedade.
Entendemos, a cada dia mais, que o fazer educativo é, por natureza, um ato político. Ser educadora é abraçar a responsabilidade de não fechar os olhos para as vulnerabilidades que atravessam os muros da escola e fazer do acolhimento, da escuta ativa e da sensibilidade os primeiros passos para a garantia da dignidade dos nossos estudantes.
É movida por essa necessidade urgente de educar para a vida em comum que a Rede Brasileira de Educação em Direitos Humanos – Coordenação Minas Gerais (ReBEDH-MG) mantém seu compromisso e atua neste espaço. Fortalecer o estudo, o debate e as práticas pedagógicas voltadas para os direitos humanos é o nosso caminho para romper os ciclos históricos de exclusão que muitas vezes se repetem entre as gerações.
Os direitos humanos não podem ser tratados apenas como ideias abstratas; eles precisam ganhar corpo nas políticas públicas, no chão das escolas, nos locais de trabalho e nas nossas relações diárias.
Educar para os direitos humanos é, acima de tudo, um compromisso permanente com a transformação. É lutar por uma sociedade em que a dignidade não seja privilégio de poucos, mas a realidade viva de todos.

title: GRAY Network’s Menstrual Health project transforms education in Central and South Tongu
content:
Audio By Carbonatix
A menstrual hygiene project initiated by GRAY Network has significantly promoted inclusive education in the Central and South Tongu Districts in the Volta Region.
The project led to decreased absenteeism, increased confidence, and a safe, supportive environment for young girls to thrive both in school and within their communities.
It was titled Strengthening Volunteer-Led Sexual and Reproductive Health and Rights (SRHR), Menstrual Hygiene Management (MHM), and Life Skills Education in Schools and Communities, sponsored by STAR-Ghana Foundation.
School-based Menstrual Hygiene Management Clubs were established as part of the initiative, where community sensitisation sessions were held, and parents were engaged.
Implementation of the project introduced young females to producing reusable sanitary facilities, provided with menstrual hygiene kits, trained volunteers to supervise beneficiaries, and distributed reusable sanitary pads to adolescent girls.
Through a unique volunteer-led approach, GRAY Network trained teachers, nurses, community health volunteers, seamstresses, and peer educators to deliver comprehensive education on menstrual hygiene management, sexual and reproductive health and rights, life skills, and gender equality.
The project, piloted at Atsieve D/A Basic School and Lakpo D/A Basic School, has demonstrated that investing in menstrual health promotes quality education, gender equality, and contributes to shaping the country’s future.
Beyond improving girls' participation in education, the initiative has transformed school culture. Boys who took part in the educational sessions developed a better understanding of menstruation, challenged harmful myths, reduced teasing, and became active supporters of their female classmates.
Teachers in the beneficiary schools described this positive behavioural change as a major factor in creating safer, more respectful, and inclusive learning environments.
They explained that the clubs have grown into platforms that not only provide menstrual health education but also foster leadership, communication, public speaking, peer mentoring, and advocacy skills among students.
These clubs continue to empower learners to educate one another while promoting dignity and gender equality within their schools.
The impact of the project extends beyond classrooms into homes and communities, with parents reporting improved understanding of menstrual hygiene, better communication with their daughters, reduced household expenditure on sanitary products, and increased confidence in supporting girls throughout their education.
Families also indicated that savings from reusable sanitary pads are now being redirected towards educational expenses such as books, uniforms, school bags, and future Senior High School education.
According to Madam Esinam Tekpor, the South Tongu District Girl Child Coordinator of the Ghana Education Service, the intervention has significantly improved the overall school environment.
"Education cannot be achieved when learners face barriers that prevent them from participating fully in school. This project has demonstrated that addressing menstrual health is essential to ensuring every child has an equal opportunity to learn, participate, and succeed,” she said.
She mentioned that teachers across the beneficiary schools unanimously reported positive changes among girls following the intervention.
“They observed increased confidence, regular school attendance, improved classroom participation, stronger relationships with teachers, greater willingness to discuss menstrual health issues, and better academic engagement,” she added.
She also highlighted a significant reduction in menstruation-related absenteeism after girls gained access to reusable sanitary pads and menstrual hygiene education.
She stressed that sustainable educational progress requires collaboration among schools, families, health institutions, and community partners.
"What makes this initiative exceptional is that it goes beyond distributing reusable sanitary pads. It strengthens the entire educational ecosystem by engaging teachers, parents, community leaders, health professionals, and students themselves. When communities work together, schools become safer, more inclusive, and more responsive to the needs of every learner."

title: [Research] AI-Driven Optimization of Renewable Energy Systems in Ethiopia: A National Framework
content: The study proposes artificial intelligence (AI) based framework for enhancing the performance and operational efficiency of renewable energy systems in Ethiopia. By considering the country’s abundant resource such as solar, wind, and hydropower, the framework combines advanced machine learning and intelligent optimization techniques, including Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) networks, Extreme Gradient Boosting (XGBoost), and Reinforcement Learning (RL), to address the main challenges associated with renewable energy integration and grid management system. The proposed method utilizes a real-world meteorological and energy production datasets obtained from Ethiopian Electric Power (EEP) and national meteorological agencies to develop accurate forecasting and decision-support models. Experimental result shows that the optimized XGBoost model achieved the highest predictive accuracy value of 0.91 and a Mean Absolute Error (MAE) of 0.099, while the LSTM model attained a value of 0.89 and an MAE of 0.112, and the RL-based optimization strategy improved grid stability by approximately 10% and reduced energy losses by 15%, highlighting its effectiveness in supporting intelligent energy management. By takling the critical issues such as renewable energy intermittency, transmission inefficiencies, and the growing demand for decentralized energy solutions, the proposed framework gives a practical pathway toward a more resilient and sustainable energy infrastructure across the country and beyond. The study contributes to Ethiopia’s ongoing energy transition efforts and support broader sustainable development goal through improved energy reliability, environmental sustainability, and expanded access to affordable and clean electricity.

title: Côte d’Ivoire-AIP/ La communication hospitalière au service de la qualité des soins à Lakota
content:
Lakota, 21 sept 2026 (AIP) – L’amélioration de l’environnement hospitalier et de l’offre des soins à l’hôpital général de Lakota s’améliorent grâce à une dynamique soutenue par le service de communication de cet Etablissement public hospitalier départemental (EPHD) dirigé par Guina Joël, a constaté l’AIP.
En service à Lakota depuis mai 2023, M. Guina, rencontré sur son lieu de travail, a animé un plateau improvisé destiné aux plateformes WhatsApp et au profil Facebook de l’EPHD de Lakota. À cette occasion,
il a conduit un entretien face caméra avec le point focal Qualité de l’établissement, le technicien biologique Klai Koutou Élysée, autour de la question de la qualité de l’accueil et des soins.
Selon lui, la diffusion de messages clairs sur les services, les procédures et les droits des patients permet de réduire les malentendus et de renforcer l’adhésion aux traitements. Les campagnes de sensibilisation qu’il pilote, axées sur la prévention et l’hygiène, contribuent à améliorer la santé publique et à diminuer la pression sur les services hospitaliers. En outre, ces actions renforcent la confiance de la communauté envers l’établissement.
M. Guina a souligné que la qualité ne se limite pas à l’aspect technique mais englobe aussi la dimension humaine, avec une communication transparente envers les patients, le respect de leur dignité, l’implication des familles et l’instauration d’un climat de confiance. Il estime que la valorisation du travail des soignants
accroît leur motivation, tandis qu’une communication ouverte avec la société et les partenaires renforce la crédibilité de l’hôpital.
Lors de la 4è édition de la Semaine des communicateurs en santé (SCOM-2025), tenue du 27 au 29 novembre 2025 à Yamoussoukro, Guina Joël a été distingué 2è meilleur chargé de communication national des hôpitaux généraux et centres hospitaliers régionaux de Côte d’Ivoire, une reconnaissance de son engagement en faveur d’une communication hospitalière au service de la qualité des soins.

title: Cities get more say in data center development under new California laws
content:
Dive Brief:
-
California Gov. Gavin Newsom on Monday signed seven bills aimed at giving communities more information about proposed data centers’ energy, water, workforce and land use to help weigh their economic costs and benefits.
-
The new laws require data centers “pay their fair share of grid update costs,” disclose water use to local governments and give up eligibility for blanket environmental exemptions, according to the governor’s office.
-
They come on the heels of Los Angeles County’s planning director ordering a temporary ban on development of large-scale AI data centers in unincorporated areas of California’s most populous county, according to multiple news reports.
Dive Insight:
California is home to 296 data centers, the third highest number in the U.S., according to Data Center Map.
“Communities are left to deal with the consequences — higher electricity demand, grid constraints, water use, and pollution,” Newsom said in a statement. “With these laws, we are ensuring that Californians remain in the driver’s seat — and that those profiting from data centers aren’t doing so at our expense.”
The bills Newsom signed Monday include:
SB 1168: Directs the California Public Utilities Commission to examine data centers’ energy use and ensure they pay for transmission and distribution upgrades and load increases. “Californians’ utility bills are already among the highest in the nation, and the rapid growth of data centers is threatening to send rates through the roof,” state Sen. Jerry McNerney, the bill’s sponsor, said in a statement.
SB 886 and SB 887: Require data centers to pay all infrastructure upgrade and generation costs, bear a larger share of wildfire mitigation and liability costs, and undergo environmental review. The bills will also ensure local communities have a say in data center projects, according to a news release from state Sen. Steve Padilla, the bills’ sponsor. “These are some of the nation’s strongest data center ratepayer protections — stopping Big Tech from sticking California families with the bill for their data centers,” Padilla said in a statement.
AB 1577: Requires monthly reporting of data centers’ energy consumption and efficiency metrics to the California Energy Commission and estimated energy usage to local agencies as part of permitting.
AB 2383: Incentivizes data centers to use onsite clean energy resources to help California “responsibly plan for the future of our electrical grid while keeping electricity costs down for consumers,” the bill’s sponsor, Assemblyman Rick Chavez Zbur, said in a statement.
AB 2469 and AB 2619: Strengthen oversight of data center water use by requiring potential data center developers to complete a water supply assessment and develop a water scarcity plan during permitting and establishing a statewide water reporting requirement to obtain and renew business licenses. “Every drop counts,” Assemblymember Diane Papan, chair of the Assembly Water Committee and sponsor of the bills, said in a statement. “We cannot manage what we do not measure.”

title: Meet Elavenil Valarivan: Batman-Bandana Shooter Wins Two Asian Games Silvers
content:
Elavenil Valarivan, 27, won two silver medals for India in the women’s 10m air rifle events at the Aichi-Nagoya Asian Games on September 20, 2026, ending an eight-year wait for an Asian Games podium.
She first helped India finish second in the team event alongside Sonam Uttam Maskar and Vidarsa K Vinod, with their combined 1898.0 points behind China’s world-record 1904.2. Hours later, Valarivan claimed individual silver with 252.4, finishing just 0.6 behind Japan’s Hinata Taichi, who set an Asian Games record of 253.0.
The result is particularly significant for the two-time Olympian, who had previously competed at Jakarta 2018, Tokyo 2020 and Paris 2024 without an Asian Games medal.
Rather than blaming pressure for the narrow individual loss, Valarivan said she was focused on following her technique and process, while acknowledging that greater patience and better breathing could have changed her final shots.
Her journey from a teenager who discovered shooting almost by chance to a world-ranked elite shooter reflects years of coaching, setbacks, self-doubt and a gradual shift from chasing results to enjoying the sport.
The Shooter Behind The Bandana
Valarivan’s distinctive appearance has become almost as recognisable as her shooting. A Batman bandana sits beneath her visor, while small gold earrings reflect her Tamil roots. Yet behind the personality is a shooter trained to control the smallest details.
In 10m air rifle, the ISSF’s 10-ring is just 0.5 mm across, while competitors must maintain extraordinary control over their posture, breathing, trigger movement and concentration. Valarivan discovered shooting at around 13 after accompanying her father to a range and eventually began training seriously.
Her rise was rapid: in 2018, aged 18, she won junior World Cup gold in Sydney and recorded a 631.4 qualification score that was then a junior world record. She later trained at Gagan Narang’s academy under coach Neha Chavan, developing into one of India’s leading rifle shooters.
Narang has remained a mentor, and before the Asian Games final, he video-called Valarivan and shared advice. Valarivan said his guidance helped her approach the final with greater perspective.
Eight Years Of Setbacks
The two silvers carry the weight of several disappointments. At her first Asian Games in Jakarta in 2018, Valarivan finished 14th in the women’s 10m air rifle and missed the final. She was subsequently left out of India’s Hangzhou Asian Games team.
At the Tokyo Olympics, she finished 16th in individual qualification, while at Paris 2024 she placed 10th and again missed the final. Yet major international success continued. She won the Asian Championship in 2025 with a 253.6 final, an Asian record at the time, and successfully defended her title in New Delhi in February 2026 with 252.0.
The ISSF also records her as part of India’s world-record mixed-team performance with Arjun Babuta at the 2026 Asian Rifle/Pistol Championship, where they scored 505.0. Valarivan has acknowledged that self-doubt was part of the journey, particularly when results did not match the work being put in.
She credited her coach, psychologist, strength and conditioning trainer, nutritionist and physiotherapist for helping her through those difficult periods. Her approach has since changed. “Initially it was more about me making it to the team, winning the competition,” she said. “Now it is more about enjoying it.”
The Logical Indian’s Perspective
Elavenil Valarivan’s story is not simply about two silver medals or a gold that slipped away by 0.6 points. It is about what happens when sporting ambition is allowed to coexist with patience, self-belief and the freedom to learn from disappointment.
Her final may have ended with silver, but her own response identifying the need for better patience, breathing and shot judgement rather than blaming pressure offers a valuable perspective on competition and resilience. Her journey also highlights the importance of the people around an athlete: coaches, psychologists, trainers, family and mentors who continue to support them when medals do not arrive immediately.
